claim: Riemann's theta-integral construction, the later separation of gamma and pole artifacts, and the affine substitution s=1/2+it form one normalization chain: completion makes the reflection s↦1−s exact, while centering at its fixed line converts RH into reality of the zeros of an even entire function of t.
historical_or_program_relation: The original split-reflect-center integral makes symmetry visible; the later completed-xi formulation isolates precisely which zeta zeros remain and packages that symmetry as the modern real-rootedness formulation.
limits: Completion and evenness constrain zero geometry but do not establish that zeros exist on, or all lie on, the critical line; the confinement argument also depends on prior Euler-product nonvanishing and the functional equation.
title: Completion turns reflection symmetry into a real-rootedness problem

claim: Taking the logarithm of the Euler product makes multiplicative prime-power data additive; Mellin/Perron inversion and contour residues then express its weighted summatory function through analytic singularities, especially nontrivial zeros; Möbius inversion is the separate final operation that removes prime-power repetitions to recover primes alone.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's prime-power explicit formula becomes a reusable analytic-number-theory pipeline in the later expositions: encode coefficients by a Dirichlet series, continue and shift, read residues, and only then invert the iterate structure when the target is primes rather than prime powers.
limits: The transformations require their own convergence, continuation, contour, truncation, and error estimates; a zero-sum formula neither proves RH nor licenses arbitrary rearrangement of conditionally convergent zero terms.
title: Logarithms, transforms, residues, and Möbius inversion form the prime-zero round trip

claim: The Perron kernel is not by itself a justified coefficient-sum inverse: in the full contour proof, subtracting the pre-cutoff terms and shifting by the first surviving exponent creates the horizontal-edge decay, whereas truncating the vertical integral replaces exact inversion by a quantified loss concentrated near the cutoff discontinuity.
historical_or_program_relation: The exact generalized-Dirichlet-series argument identifies representation design as the decay mechanism; the modern truncated form exposes contour height T as a resolution budget and makes that same transform usable in explicit estimates.
limits: The exact and truncated formulas have different hypotheses and conclusions, the half-weight at a jump is part of the inversion convention, and neither form supplies analytic continuation or zero-free information on its own.
title: Perron inversion trades sharp cutoffs against decay and finite-frequency resolution

claim: Critical-line sign changes and Rolle-interlaced derivative zeros provide local witnesses, while the argument principle supplies an exhaustive multiplicity count; equality of the two closes the classification. In large computations, rigorous sign-error margins, endpoint closure, count identities, and targeted reruns are the additional interfaces that make this abstract witness-plus-count architecture a finite certificate.
historical_or_program_relation: The same proof pattern appears in analytic classification of derivative zeros and in finite RH verification, with computation adding explicit control of floating-point signs and bookkeeping vulnerabilities to the classical argument-principle closure.
limits: The derivative-zero classification is a different region and object from critical-line zeta verification; the computational conclusion is finite-height only, and overlap across related implementations is not the same as independently developed verification.
title: Local zero witnesses become complete only when matched to a global count

claim: A certified zero count through height H covers the low spectral range, an explicit zero-free inequality covers heights above H, and choosing its parameter at the crossover turns the two inputs into one hypothesis for a shifted-contour explicit-formula bound; published finite-range estimates and a terminal computation then patch the remaining small-x intervals.
historical_or_program_relation: Large-scale zero verification was reused not as evidence for global RH but as one bounded component of an explicit prime-number-theorem estimate, with contour optimization and range patching carrying the information from zeros to ψ and related functions.
limits: Finite RH verification does not imply the full hypothesis, the asymptotic region remains essential above H, and the resulting constants inherit the stated verification, numerical-error, monotonicity, and explicit-formula assumptions.
title: A verified zero range and an asymptotic zero-free region can be spliced into an all-range prime bound

claim: In an unsmoothed explicit formula, vertical contour truncation induces a canonical magnitude ordering of zero terms and that ordering is part of the formula. Mellin smoothing instead makes the logarithmic-derivative identity absolutely convergent enough to integrate and exponentiate into prime and zero factors; changing the cutoff moves contribution between those factors while their product is designed to remain stable.
historical_or_program_relation: The conditional-summation warning already present in Riemann's expansion becomes a design criterion for later numerical reconstruction and motivates the smoothed hybrid Euler-Hadamard representation.
limits: Smoothing changes the represented observable and does not justify rearranging the original series; the reported cutoff compensation is a numerical representation check, not by itself a proof of the hybrid theorem or of RH.
title: Smoothing replaces a conditionally ordered zero sum by a stable prime-zero factorization

claim: The logarithmic derivative and explicit formula naturally produce weighted prime powers, so retaining them avoids an unnecessary Möbius inversion during zero-based reconstruction. For log-value statistics, however, the averaging family decides their role: higher powers and squares are negligible errors in the height family, while prime squares survive quadratic-character averaging and create the symplectic mean shift.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's separation of primes from repetitions develops into a representation-selection rule: keep prime powers when they diagonalize the prime-zero transform, but decompose them by exponent when family averaging can promote one layer into a leading statistic.
limits: The height and quadratic-character families have different averaging symmetries, so negligibility in one cannot be transferred to the other; retaining prime powers reconstructs a weighted density, not the ordinary prime indicator.
title: Prime powers switch from native signal to removable or structural terms according to the representation

claim: Connes's quotient construction makes zeros arise as the distributional support left when multiplication by an L-factor fails to force density, whereas the difference-operator proposal obtains Hurwitz-zeta formal eigenfunctions and imposes boundary evaluation to select zeta zeros. Comparing them isolates the decisive Hilbert–Pólya obligation: construct a natural domain, adjoint, and completeness theory that produces the zero condition without defining the space from the desired spectrum.
historical_or_program_relation: Both programs move beyond a bare list of eigenvalues to an operator-space mechanism, but the answer-encoding diagnostic in the trace-formula program sharply exposes the unresolved inverse choice and boundary-domain work in the formal Hamiltonian proposal.
limits: The Connes support classification is not a self-adjoint operator with the zeros as ordinary eigenvalues, while the difference-operator similarity is formal and noninvertible on periodic functions; neither unit establishes spectral reality or RH.
title: A spectral zero model is judged by whether zeros emerge from its domain rather than being encoded into it

claim: The completed functional equation and modified PT symmetry both organize zeros or proposed eigenvalues into reflected/conjugate pairs, but neither pairing forces fixed-line location or real spectrum. The missing strengthening must be something like a legitimate self-adjoint domain or a geometrically forced sign condition, not another restatement of symmetry.
historical_or_program_relation: Classical completion identifies the symmetry that RH would sharpen; random-matrix and finite-field analogies suggest self-adjointness or negativity, while the PT construction demonstrates concretely why a weaker pairing symmetry can remain compatible with off-line zeros.
limits: PT is analyzed only for proposed formal states, the finite-field and random-matrix comparisons do not transfer a classical operator or intersection form, and naming self-adjointness or negativity does not construct either mechanism.
title: Spectral pairing symmetries do not supply the sign or self-adjointness needed for RH

claim: Fourier inversion expresses a theta kernel through Xi so that even derivatives become moments used to amplify an eventual sign, while a theta-tail Laplace representation makes the central Taylor coefficients positive moments whose finite windows form Jensen polynomials. Saddle-controlled coefficient ratios then prove an eventual Hermite hyperbolicity regime, whereas the exact all-degree, all-shift hyperbolicity family is equivalent to RH.
historical_or_program_relation: The older moment-sign route uses theta structure to force infinitely many critical-line zeros; the Jensen program repackages related central derivative data into algebraically testable finite polynomials and separates universal Hermite behavior from the unresolved global criterion.
limits: The frozen older unit stops before its final contradiction, eventual Jensen hyperbolicity is much weaker than hyperbolicity for every required degree and shift, and neither an asymptotic Hermite limit nor infinitely many line zeros proves RH.
title: Theta-derived moments feed two different finite encodings of xi zero geometry

claim: Unfolded zeta zeros and characteristic-polynomial spectra share local statistical behavior after the mean density is removed, but moment constants and mesoscopic covariance retain Euler-product information: the arithmetic factor must be added separately, and near one the logarithmic zeta pole generated by coherent primes sets the covariance scale.
historical_or_program_relation: Random-matrix evidence shifts from a Hilbert–Pólya clue to one component of hybrid models; the mismatch in moment constants and the prime derivation of covariance identify exactly which information the spectral universal model forgets.
limits: Statistical agreement does not construct the missing classical cohomology or self-adjoint operator, the arithmetic factorization is model-dependent, and the cited covariance result is finite-dimensional and does not establish a pathwise field or RH.
title: Random matrices model local zero correlations while prime structure supplies missing arithmetic factors

claim: For a smoothed summatory error, tail bounds and finite-dimensional phase alignment can let one low zero pair force oscillation. By contrast, reconstructing localized prime-power peaks from a Gaussian-smoothed explicit formula requires a broad, correctly ordered frequency band: ordinates determine peak locations, real parts determine amplitudes, and the zero cutoff fixes the reliable spatial range.
historical_or_program_relation: The two uses of zeros expose complementary transform regimes—low-frequency certification of a global oscillation and high-bandwidth synthesis of local arithmetic detail—so the number of zeros required is controlled by smoothing and target resolution rather than by one universal cutoff rule.
limits: The observables, kernels, and error goals differ; empirical reconstruction endpoints do not bound the full omitted tail, while phase-alignment oscillation does not recover individual primes or locate the first sign reversal.
title: Smoothing determines whether a few zeros certify oscillation or many zeros resolve prime peaks

claim: A computation can certify every zero in a bounded rectangle while remaining silent about a limiting Gram-block law or global RH; independently, iterated-logarithm growth shows how a rigorously unbounded zero-driven term can remain visually flat long enough for an opposing finite-range prime-count bias to dominate all feasible data.
historical_or_program_relation: The growth of verified-height computations strengthens bounded certificates, while later oscillation theory explains why extending those bounds cannot by itself settle asymptotic sign or probabilistic behavior.
limits: Slow eventual oscillation does not undermine a correct finite certificate, the cited decomposition of the bias is heuristic in form, no first reversal is located, and the observed Gram distributions are not proved to converge.
title: Exact finite certification and asymptotic inference answer different questions

claim: Taylor polynomialization, Hölder duplication, Vinogradov mean values, and rational approximation first produce cancellation in short sums of n^(−it); blockwise Abel summation transfers that saving to zeta near one; Euler-product positivity and local zero terms then convert the zeta bound into zero exclusion; finally a shifted Perron contour turns the zero-free region into a prime-number-theorem error term.
historical_or_program_relation: This analytic program records a causal chain from oscillatory-sum technology to prime distribution, with each stage changing representation and exposing a new proof obligation rather than treating an improved PNT error as a direct consequence of a single estimate.
limits: Every transfer is range- and parameter-dependent, the local zero-repulsion and final contour estimates require their stated growth bounds, and the resulting unconditional error remains far from the square-root scale that RH would imply.
title: Short-sum cancellation reaches primes only through a sequence of representation interfaces

claim: Critical-line sign changes provide a lower count of zeros with the desired location, while an argument-principle-style global count supplies the exhaustive total; equality closes the off-line completeness gap. Once that equality is the proof target, a computation may retain certified sign-change counts without refining and storing every zero ordinate.
historical_or_program_relation: The early Hutchinson-Backlund pattern of matching located witnesses to a rectangle-wide count is the same certificate architecture later made scalable by count-only verification: algorithmic savings come from discarding location detail that the final count comparison does not use.
limits: Sign changes alone are not exhaustive, and the count-only unit does not itself contain its surrounding global completeness proof. The conclusion remains bounded by the certified height or rectangle, and none of these units turns finite agreement into RH at all heights.
title: Finite RH verification composes witness counts with an independent total

claim: A computed Hardy-Z value yields a rigorous sign only when its magnitude exceeds a method-specific absolute-error envelope. This inequality naturally triages the computation: certify large-margin samples cheaply, and route small-margin cases to slower evaluation or shifted sampling, while recording that shifting changes the measurement protocol and subsequent aggregation.
historical_or_program_relation: Lehmer's SWAC-era remainder-aware screening anticipates later range computations that budget interpolation, analytic truncation, and machine arithmetic separately; later shifted-point runs make explicit that numerical stabilization also creates a bookkeeping confound.
limits: The cited error bounds are tied to particular formulas, machines, and height ranges. Shifted evaluation is not an independent implementation, a stable-looking sign is not a rigorous sign without its bound, and certified sample signs do not by themselves certify that all zeros were counted.
title: An error envelope turns uncertain samples into an adaptive evaluation policy

claim: Choosing the Riemann-Siegel saddle scale reduces a critical-line evaluation to a square-root-length cosine sum with correction terms; precomputed Taylor tables can make those corrections cheap across repeated calls. For the fast representation to support proof, its series truncation, interpolation, coefficient truncation, and floating-point or interval errors must still be converted into a conservative sign margin.
historical_or_program_relation: The computational program progresses by moving work from runtime into analytic specialization and symbolic preprocessing, then by restoring epistemic control through explicit method-specific error accounting; rigorous multiprecision therefore changes both throughput and what the output certifies.
limits: The Taylor-table unit does not provide a uniform bound for its coefficient cutoff, and the later error envelopes apply to their stated implementations rather than automatically validating Pugh's tables. Cross-machine or GHz-hour rates are not comparable without accounting for sampling density, hardware, precision, and rigor.
title: Riemann-Siegel speedups form a ladder from analytic compression to certified arithmetic

claim: An FFT-based method can accelerate a long batch without improving the latency of one adaptively requested Z evaluation, while a processed-height-per-GHz-hour metric can hide the number of samples, precision, and proof obligations per unit height. Computational design must therefore match the cost metric to contiguous verification or sparse exception resolution.
historical_or_program_relation: Large verification campaigns favor amortized batch transforms, whereas exception-driven searches expose the remaining cost of an individual Dirichlet sum; the later rigorous-computation comparison shows why hardware-normalized throughput still does not erase this objective split.
limits: The units do not provide a controlled head-to-head benchmark or select a universally superior algorithm. The conclusion concerns optimization objectives, not mathematical correctness, and any proposed low-latency approximation would still need to fit the existing analytic error budget.
title: Batch throughput and single-point latency are different optimization targets

claim: Near-cancellation in a critical-line evaluation can guide a targeted search toward an unusually close zero pair, but raw closeness is only discovery evidence. After rescaling ordinates into the heat-family coordinates, separately rounded bounds for the pair's surrounding zero interactions must compose into the scalar Lehmer inequality before the pair has dynamical significance.
historical_or_program_relation: Lehmer's recurrence-guided proposal to inspect remote stress regions develops into a discovery-to-certificate loop: broad computation finds a candidate, high precision is concentrated in its window, and analytic local, intermediate, and tail bounds qualify it for a de Bruijn-Newman lower bound.
limits: Recurrence of a cancellation pattern is not recurrence of RH counterexamples, the targeted window is not an exhaustive optimum search, and the certificate concerns the selected pair and a lower bound for Lambda rather than RH or the global distribution of close gaps.
title: A cancellation heuristic becomes useful only after a global-interaction certificate

claim: The Lehmer-pair criterion refuses to treat an adjacent gap in isolation: its static certificate normalizes the gap by an interaction term involving the remaining zeros. Heat-flow analysis supplies the dynamical counterpart, an inverse-distance evolution in which every real zero moves under the surrounding configuration; only after the environmental term is uniformly controlled can a vanishing-gap sequence drive phase-boundary bounds toward zero.
historical_or_program_relation: Pair-based lower bounds turn exceptional static configurations into finite instability certificates, while the later interacting-particle reframing explains why gap relaxation and near-lattice behavior are inherently nonlocal rather than properties of two ordinates alone.
limits: The static Lehmer criterion and the heat-flow ODE are distinct results, and this relation does not derive either from the other. The particle relaxation and unrenormalized Hamiltonian discussion is heuristic at this stage, while the infinite-pair conclusion is conditional on an infinite sequence of certified pairs with the required controlled parameters.
title: A close gap is dynamically meaningful only relative to the other zeros

claim: A verified-height RH computation becomes an upper bound for the de Bruijn-Newman constant only through a threshold theorem, whereas a certified close-pair configuration becomes a lower bound through a pair-specific instability formula. The phase boundary therefore accepts two different computational inputs with opposite inequality directions: exhaustive coverage below a height and an exceptional local witness.
historical_or_program_relation: Extending zero verification improves a globally transferred upper bound, while searching later ranges for stronger certified gaps improves lower bounds; together they turn computation from undirected RH evidence into two theorem-mediated boundary-measurement programs.
limits: The inputs, transfer theorems, and inequality directions must not be conflated. The stated verified height licenses Lambda at most 0.2 but not the next threshold or RH, and any finite close-pair result supplies only its stated lower bound; neither computation alone pins the boundary at zero.
title: Finite computations constrain Lambda through two logically opposite interfaces

claim: Both finite RH verification and the Jensen-polynomial obstruction search avoid approximating every complex root, but their count logic is dual. For zeta, an on-line witness count matching an independent total excludes additional off-line zeros in a bounded region; for a Jensen polynomial, a complete real-root count below the degree establishes that some roots are nonreal and hence supplies an existential obstruction.
historical_or_program_relation: The older contour-count-plus-sign-change architecture and the later Sturm-chain computation share a decision-oriented compression of root data, yet one proves absence by equality while the other proves existence by deficit.
limits: A Sturm theorem for exact coefficients is distinct from floating-point Sturm-sign evaluation, so interval coverage and sign stability remain separate obligations. The zeta count is analytic and region-bounded, the Jensen count is algebraic and polynomial-specific, and the analogy transfers certificate logic rather than either theorem's hypotheses.
title: Root counting replaces root location with opposite logical polarity in two programs

claim: Landau's inexpensive polynomial score can rank candidates differently from the full finite zero-free-region constant, just as an outer-first Gram-block search policy tuned to common short blocks loses efficiency on rare long blocks. In both cases, the cheap stage should generate or order candidates, while task-specific evaluation or a conditional branch determines the final choice.
historical_or_program_relation: The zero-free-region search retains diverse near-optimal surrogate polynomials and reruns the expensive R0 calculation; the zero-verification search uses empirical block type and length to identify where a once-effective query order should branch. Both are corrections to optimizing a proxy as though its ranking were invariant.
limits: This is a shared computational-design relation, not a claim that polynomial optimization and zero search have the same mathematics. Neither source proves a global optimizer: the polynomial pool is finite and expanded heuristically, while the Gram-block distributions and strategy crossover are empirical and range-dependent.
title: Cheap computational surrogates must be reranked against the downstream objective

claim: Across the deterministic and generalized Nyman–Beurling criteria, the decisive bridge is not approximation by itself but an admissible Mellin evaluation: a putative zeta zero annihilates the transforms of the approximating span while the target transform remains nonzero. Mellin–Plancherel domination, mean-cancelling compactification, and splitting the domain at one are three concrete ways of making that evaluation continuous along the claimed closure.
historical_or_program_relation: The broad density formulation is refined first into a norm-preserving spectral factorization and later into explicit continuity templates for generalized or random kernels. This progression isolates the reusable zero-exclusion mechanism from the particular fractional-part dictionary.
limits: The continuity hypotheses are not interchangeable: the Baez-Duarte argument uses RH-dependent domination in one direction, the compact-support argument proves only zero-set inclusion unless the kernel Mellin transform is separately nonzero, and the probabilistic criterion has its own tail conditions. No one of these units proves RH or transfers every kernel between frameworks.
title: Mellin evaluation turns closure into a zero-annihilator test

claim: Damping the natural Möbius sums identifies the correct pointwise target and preserves each fixed coordinate, while smoothing also makes the far tail estimable; neither operation by itself supplies convergence in the Nyman–Beurling Hilbert norm. In the coordinate formulation, the unresolved mass is localized concretely to a moving intermediate window, so regularization relocates rather than removes the proof burden.
historical_or_program_relation: The strengthened Baez-Duarte criterion recasts natural approximation as a summability scheme; later coordinate analysis explains why that scheme can look locally successful yet still lack a global square-summable dominator. Proposed Cesaro or subsequence variants continue this regularization program but remain epistemically separate from the proved damped criterion.
limits: Pointwise convergence, fixed-coordinate convergence, and far-tail bounds do not imply norm convergence. The accepted record proves equivalence only for the specified damped family; the proposed Cesaro, subsequence, rate, and Lp variants are not promoted here to equivalent criteria.
title: Regularization fixes local limits while leaving the Hilbert-norm bottleneck

claim: Restrictions or enlargements of a Nyman–Beurling dictionary preserve an RH implication only when the information they discard is audited in the relevant direction. The smaller antisymmetric difference space remains equivalent because the lost fractional-part component is quantitatively restored; the strong-kernel necessity route can drop Mellin nonvanishing, whereas the sufficiency route obtains only zero-set inclusion until nonvanishing is supplied separately.
historical_or_program_relation: These sources replace a single canonical generator family by symmetry-adapted, analytic-kernel, and probabilistic variants. Their combined lesson is a concrete design rule: necessity may tolerate a broader kernel class than sufficiency, and an apparently smaller space is safe only when its missing direction is controlled rather than silently quotiented out.
limits: The HP correction argument, the strong-kernel theorem directions, and the pNB/gNB examples use different spaces and hypotheses. They do not establish a common maximal dictionary, and the probabilistic examples explicitly show that a condition needed by one formulation need not classify another.
title: Changing the approximation dictionary is direction-specific

claim: The probabilistic extension is connected to the deterministic strong Nyman–Beurling program by a representation identity: expectation of a fractional-part dilation becomes the negative Müntz transform of the law's survival function. Thus randomness enters through a deterministic kernel and moment-controlled norm estimates, while the earlier sum-integral/pseudo-convolution identity supplies the operator language into which that kernel can be placed.
historical_or_program_relation: The later probabilistic formulation does not merely average approximation errors; it re-encodes a probability law as a deterministic transform compatible with an established dilation-and-convolution framework. This turns distributional choices into analyzable kernel choices.
limits: The records do not state that every survival function is a strong kernel or that the 2005 closure theorems automatically apply to every random law. Moment conditions, tail regularity, and the separate pNB/gNB hypotheses remain genuine admissibility gates.
title: Expectation converts random dilations into deterministic Müntz kernels

claim: The Farey RH criteria become concrete only after two representation choices are fixed: Möbius inversion removes coprimality, and empirical-rank centering subtracts the correct deterministic triangular contribution. With that centering, Franel's quadratic discrepancy can be transformed through Bernoulli–Möbius coordinates and cyclic Dedekind symmetrization into gcd-weighted cancellation; replacing rank by interval length loses an uncontrolled residue-class fluctuation.
historical_or_program_relation: The overview's aggregate discrepancy criterion is refined by the earlier Farey analysis into the exact combinatorial and correlation mechanisms that carry it. This identifies why the L2 statistic is arithmetic rather than merely a generic equidistribution norm.
limits: The mechanism supports the Farey discrepancy side only. It supplies no bridge to the distinct cyclotomic-height criterion mentioned alongside it, and it does not turn a pointwise discrepancy estimate or naively centered statistic into an RH equivalence.
title: Farey discrepancy requires empirical centering before arithmetic symmetrization

claim: Robin–Lagarias and Nicolas-type criteria both concentrate multiplicative behavior on integers assembled from small primes, but their proofs live or die on effective one-sided comparison. The Robin route has incompatible RH and non-RH envelopes whose separated excess eventually outruns an elementary error term; the attempted Nicolas route combines two factors converging to compensating limits without controlling whether the deficit in one is smaller than the surplus in the other.
historical_or_program_relation: Lagarias's proof shows how a prime-product extremizer can amplify prime-counting fluctuations into a bidirectional criterion and then split finite from asymptotic obligations. The later Nicolas argument exposes the missing ingredient when the same style of packaging is supported only by a two-sided limit: sign and rate must be preserved.
limits: The criteria use different arithmetic functions and normalizations, so this is a proof-burden comparison, not an algebraic identification. The gap in the later proof does not refute the cited Nicolas equivalence or RH, and the unconditional primorial limit alone supplies neither eventual sign nor an effective rate.
title: Small-prime extremizers make one-sided rates decisive

claim: Three equivalent-criterion programs separate sharply according to what controls the unobserved tail. In the Lagarias assembly, a proved asymptotic envelope reduces the remaining obligation to an exhaustive finite prefix; for the Baez-Duarte sequence, height-suppressed coefficients can delay the dominance of a hypothetical off-line zero beyond feasible computation; in the Nicolas argument, convergence to the correct limit gives no eventual one-sided inequality at all.
historical_or_program_relation: Together these cases provide a concrete hierarchy for computational evidence: finite checking can close a theorem only after an analytic tail bound, can be weak evidence when spectral defects have delayed crossover, and cannot repair a missing sign-and-rate estimate.
limits: The delay mechanism, finite-prefix closure, and surplus-versus-deficit gap are different phenomena and supply no shared numerical cutoff. The Baez-Duarte limitation relies on its explicit zero expansion and does not assert an off-line zero; the Nicolas diagnosis concerns an argument, not the truth of its criterion.
title: Finite verification is informative only with a certified tail mechanism

claim: Both the Eisenstein-integral and Speiser analyses use Hadamard factorization followed by logarithmic differentiation to replace a multiplicative zero set with additive contributions whose sign can be controlled. In the Eisenstein setting paired zero blocks force one-dimensional unimodality of a scalar level-set function; in the Speiser setting the functional equation and gamma asymptotics orient the logarithmic-derivative field on remote contours so the argument principle can compare zero counts.
historical_or_program_relation: The shared mechanism links two otherwise different line-zero programs: local sign control can certify the number of level-set crossings, while boundary sign control can certify a global counting relation. It shows exactly how symmetry becomes operational only after a zero-product representation is differentiated.
limits: The sign domains, auxiliary functions, and conclusions differ. Unimodality of a shifted-xi level-set function does not imply a Speiser theorem, and a contour orientation argument does not transfer the Eisenstein truncation result without its separate strip geometry and parameter inequalities.
title: Logarithmic derivatives turn zero sets into sign-controlled fields

claim: Completion and a functional equation provide a global reflection architecture, but they do not by themselves classify when an RH- or Speiser-type equivalence survives. The Eisenstein construction explicitly separates modular symmetry in the geometric variable from reflection in the spectral variable, neither of which alone yields a line-zero theorem; the Speiser comparison includes both successful extensions and computational failures for functions lacking a Riemann-type equation, so absence of that equation is not a sufficient discriminator either.
historical_or_program_relation: The L-function overview treats functional equations as one half of a two-sided architecture, while the later comparison turns that architectural role into a scope boundary: additional arithmetic or finite-structure conditions must do the classifying work, though the accepted record does not yet identify them.
limits: The negative Speiser cases are reported computational evidence rather than rigorous counterexamples, and the positive class contains extra structure not isolated here. This relation neither dismisses functional symmetry nor proposes a replacement necessary-and-sufficient condition.
title: Functional symmetry is an input, not a classifier of line-zero equivalences

claim: The Baez-Duarte and Jensen criteria both translate zeta data into finite algebraic objects, but they preserve different decisive invariants. The binomial transform of reciprocal-zeta samples is tied by an exponential generating function to the Riesz entire function and carries a critical decay exponent; Jensen polynomials use finite windows of central completed-zeta coefficients and carry real-rootedness, with theta moments and uniform saddle-point ratio expansions supplying their analyzable input.
historical_or_program_relation: These are two concrete discretizations of an analytic zero problem: one makes cancellation visible as sequence decay, while the other makes it visible as coherent polynomial hyperbolicity. Their comparison identifies the representation choice—growth exponent versus root geometry—as the source of the subsequent proof burden.
limits: No accepted unit gives a transform between the two sequences, so they are not asserted to be equivalent to each other except through RH. Checking finitely many decay values or Jensen polynomials does not establish the required asymptotic bound or universal hyperbolicity, and positive theta-moment representations alone do not prove RH.
title: Finite transforms encode RH through different retained invariants

claim: Two failed analytic routes expose the same missing implication: a representation can approximate zeta or have the correct unit-modulus boundary symmetry while still lacking the interior zero-free, Hardy-norm, or positivity control needed to force critical-line zeros.
historical_or_program_relation: The counterexamples collected in the 2004 overview and the later local-factor obstruction in the semi-local operator program both turn an attractive representation into a diagnostic: the decisive burden is the stronger interior sign or norm property, not the already-visible boundary behavior.
limits: The Dirichlet-partial-sum, de Branges-space, and Hardy-space settings are mathematically distinct, so this relation does not identify one common positivity theorem or rule out repaired versions of any program.
title: Boundary symmetry and approximation repeatedly fail without interior positivity

claim: Phase normalization makes critical-line zeros detectable by real sign changes, but Gram-interval occupancy is not reliable enough to certify completeness; only agreement between an on-line witness count and an independent global zero count excludes off-line zeros in a bounded region.
historical_or_program_relation: The historical Gram-law failures forced computation away from one-root-per-cell reasoning toward neighborhood repair and then toward certificate composition: Hardy-Z sign changes supply located witnesses while the argument principle or Backlund count supplies the exhaustive cardinality.
limits: The agreement certifies only the bounded contour whose numerical errors and total count are controlled; it neither proves RH above the cutoff nor makes every individual Gram interval trustworthy.
title: Gram-point sign tests became local detectors inside a two-certificate proof

claim: Even an exhaustive finite prefix of critical-line zeros implies only a bounded-height RH statement by itself; the 2021 computation obtains an unconditional global statement about the de Bruijn-Newman constant only because a previously proved threshold theorem converts verified height into an upper bound for Lambda.
historical_or_program_relation: The relation marks a change in what large computations can license: Lehmer's census ends at its height, whereas the later verification is composed with heat-flow analysis to cross from finite certification to a global but weaker parameter bound.
limits: The transfer yields only the stated Lambda bound and does not prove RH; no amount of verified height may be described as global without the hypotheses and constants of an applicable transfer theorem.
title: A finite zero census becomes global evidence only through a separate analytic transfer

claim: The finite-field model succeeds not merely because it has correspondences, but because geometry forces a negative or positive-definite form; constructing higher-genus correspondences or semi-local trace operators without the analogous norm, index, and globally compatible normalization leaves the zero-location mechanism incomplete.
historical_or_program_relation: The historical avatar first identifies intersection-form sign as a working mechanism, the higher-genus reconstruction records that the carrier algebra does not automatically bring its norm, and the semi-local analytic route relocates the same obstruction to compatible principal-value normalizations in an explicit-formula trace.
limits: Divisor intersections, correspondence norms, and semi-local principal values are not identified as the same object, and the sources provide no transfer theorem from finite-field geometry to the classical zeta function.
title: The finite-field avatar isolates positivity as the missing transferable operation

claim: Matching the high-energy zeta zero count or the symplectic area of a cutoff region can preserve the leading spectral density while forgetting phase, boundary sign, and the exhaustive correspondence between every nontrivial zero and a self-adjoint spectrum that Hilbert-Polya requires.
historical_or_program_relation: Later prolate and scaling-Hamiltonian constructions realize increasingly concrete pieces of the spectral analogy, but Conrey's audit fixes the unchanged proof burden: a noncircular natural operator must account for all zeros, not merely reproduce their Weyl-scale count.
limits: Asymptotic count matching can still be structurally informative and is not evidence against the models; the relation only denies that such matching by itself proves self-adjoint spectral realization or RH.
title: Spectral counting agreement remains strictly below a Hilbert-Polya correspondence

claim: In prime-zero and phase formulas, the limiting prescription is mathematical data: changing the zero ordering, choosing a principal phase, or mismatching local principal values can alter a conditional sum, inject and cancel a zero-counting staircase, or spoil the intended global trace.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's contour-height ordering already prevents free rearrangement of the zero sum; later phase criteria reveal hidden branch corrections involving N(T), while the semi-local program identifies compatible global normalization as the obstruction to assembling canonical local traces.
limits: These are three different normalization problems, not proof that their corrections coincide or that the associated explicit formulas are invalid when their prescribed conventions are followed.
title: Ordering, branch, and principal-value conventions carry arithmetic information

claim: Farey discrepancy, cyclotomic growth, function-space density, coefficient positivity, determinants, and divisor inequalities can each encode RH exactly while exposing incompatible observables; equivalence alone supplies no mechanism connecting those observables or reason that one representation is easier to control.
historical_or_program_relation: The expanding historical catalogue of RH equivalents broadens the available interfaces, but the later comparisons make the obstruction explicit: every translation moves the hard estimate into a new norm, infinite sign family, finite determinant growth, or arithmetic inequality.
limits: The relation does not weaken the logical equivalences or preclude a criterion from becoming fruitful; it specifically rejects treating shared equivalence to RH as a demonstrated cross-method mechanism.
title: Equivalent criteria preserve truth while relocating, not removing, the proof burden

claim: For prime asymptotics, logarithmic differentiation and Tauberian transfer need nonvanishing only on Re(s)=1, whereas the explicit formula makes the stronger RH error scale depend on forcing every zero real part from the boundary value 1 down to 1/2.
historical_or_program_relation: The successful prime-number-theorem route isolates a minimal analytic boundary condition and a theorem that returns to counting; later explicit-formula accounts show precisely why that historical success does not close the sharper zero-location burden posed by RH.
limits: This relation proves no new zero-free region and does not say that Tauberian methods cannot contribute to RH; it distinguishes the zero control sufficient for the two stated conclusions.
title: The Tauberian bridge explains why PNT needs less zero control than RH

claim: Finite Jensen or Lehmer-pair certificates establish lower bounds on Lambda through exceptional local obstructions, but the proof that Lambda is nonnegative uses a different quantifier: any negative-time real-zero phase would force almost all normalized gaps toward a lattice, contradicting a positive proportion of small zeta gaps.
historical_or_program_relation: The program moves from computationally finding one obstruction at a chosen deformation time, through pair-specific heat-flow bounds, to a dynamical-energy argument that rules out the entire negative-time regime by aggregate gap behavior.
limits: A failed finite witness search proves nothing, and no collection of the cited finite certificates alone yields Lambda>=0; the collective argument additionally depends on its heat-flow analysis and the external small-gap theorem.
title: Newman lower bounds progressed from exceptional witnesses to collective gap rigidity

claim: Near-cancellation and an unusually small raw gap motivate targeted computation, but a pair affects the de Bruijn-Newman boundary only after scaling to the heat-family coordinates and bounding its interaction with the full zero configuration through g_k with one-sided numerical control.
historical_or_program_relation: Lehmer's 1956 close-zero phenomenon supplied a search heuristic; the 1993 work turned such a discovered pair into a compositional certificate whose local high-precision window, remote-zero bounds, and upward-rounded sum establish the Lehmer criterion and hence a Lambda lower bound.
limits: The recurrence heuristic neither predicts an RH counterexample nor proves search optimality, and a certified pair supplies only its stated lower bound rather than exhaustive information about all zeros or the exact value of Lambda.
title: A close zero pair became relevant only after its global environment was certified

claim: The transferable random-matrix object is not an arbitrary deterministic unitary polynomial but a symmetry class and probability law selected by an arithmetic L-function family; rare deterministic counterexamples can coexist with statistical predictions, while any deeper model must still reproduce irregular gaps and exceptional multiplicities rather than smoothing them away.
historical_or_program_relation: Early spacing correlations suggested a missing spectral or cohomological structure, Katz-Sarnak supplied the family-to-compact-group mechanism in the finite-field model, and later analogy audits separated model-typical predictions from properties of every matrix while retaining Conrey's adequacy test for exceptional arithmetic behavior.
limits: The finite-field family theorem does not establish the classical zeta correspondence, model-conditional rarity is not an arithmetic proof, and none of these units constructs a Hilbert-Polya operator or proves RH.
title: Random-matrix evidence sharpened from spacing resemblance to a family-indexed probability law

claim: A representation can appear to generate the desired zeta symmetry or zero data while actually importing it through a critical-line parametrization, a boundary-conditioned initial state, or a branch correction containing N(T); tracing those inputs is necessary to distinguish explanation from repackaging.
historical_or_program_relation: The Hilbert-Polya audit states the noncircular correspondence requirement, the unfolded particle-in-a-box example locates the supposedly absent conjugate branch in the initial condition, and the phase criterion reveals the zero-counting staircase hidden inside principal-argument bookkeeping.
limits: Hidden structure is not automatically illegitimate if independently derived, and these examples do not rule out physical models; they identify distinct places where a claimed bridge must prove rather than assume its zeta-specific content.
title: Physical and spectral representations must audit where the target structure entered

claim: A tiny adjacent-zero gap can be a sufficient local witness for a de Bruijn-Newman lower bound once normalized by the entire zero environment, yet isolated tiny or large gaps cannot supply the positive measure required to explain the bulk Gaussian distribution of log|Z|.
historical_or_program_relation: The two programs assign the same conspicuous local event different evidentiary roles: heat-flow theory converts one certified configuration into a phase-boundary inequality, whereas the value-distribution audit tests and rejects isolated-gap dominance by comparing its available measure with Selberg-scale bulk mass.
limits: The heat-flow statement is a theorem conditional on its pair certificate, while the bulk-carrier rejection is a heuristic inconsistency argument; neither says that local gaps make no contribution outside the specific target being tested.
title: An isolated tiny gap is decisive for one interface and insufficient for another

claim: An aggregate zero-count theorem can close information missing from a local observable in two concrete ways: it can match critical-line sign-change witnesses to certify a bounded census, or it can bound the remote-zero tail in a mollified zero-free-region detector.
historical_or_program_relation: The argument-principle count first serves as the exhaustive half of finite RH verification; in the later detector architecture, a uniform N(T) remainder becomes a reusable tail-error input that lets local integral and positivity estimates be separated from distant zeros.
limits: Tail control does not locate individual zeros or prove the zero-free region by itself, and bounded census matching requires its own controlled contour evaluation; the two uses share an aggregate-count interface, not an identical proof.
title: Global zero counting was repurposed from completeness certificate to local detector control

claim: Jacobi inversion, completion, and recentering make xi entire, even, and real on the relevant axis, converting critical-line location into a real-rootedness problem; those symmetries do not produce real zeros, so later work must add a sign-change or moment-rigidity mechanism.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's cosine-kernel representation makes reflection and decay visible, the modern canonical formulation states the exact real-rootedness reduction, and the 1953 Fourier-moment route shows the additional tail-sign-to-derivative chain needed even to force infinitely many critical-line zeros.
limits: The cited moment unit stops before its intended final contradiction, and infinitely many on-line zeros would still be weaker than all zeros on the line; evenness and reality alone imply neither conclusion.
title: Completion reduced RH to real-rootedness but left sign production as the historical burden

claim: Zero alignment is unstable under changing the target value of a meromorphic function, but the de Bruijn-Newman heat deformation has a monotone real-rootedness property that compresses all times into a single phase boundary; the latter structure, not perturbation alone, makes cross-time inference possible.
historical_or_program_relation: Value-distribution theory warns that the zero fiber is exceptional among nearby a-point fibers, while the heat-family program succeeds in organizing a different deformation by an order parameter Lambda whose value at time zero is equivalent to the RH question.
limits: Changing the value a and evolving by the heat equation are different perturbations, so their stability properties are not contradictory; monotonicity defines a useful framework but does not determine Lambda or prove RH.
title: Heat flow is useful because it orders root geometry, unlike generic value perturbation

claim: Both the dynamical trace construction and the finite-field cohomological construction turn fixed points into traces by restricting or intersecting an operator graph with the diagonal. In the flow setting transversality produces the inverse determinant of one minus the return map as a local weight; in the algebraic setting the diagonal acts as an identity kernel and graph intersection becomes an alternating cohomological trace.
historical_or_program_relation: The relation identifies a concrete Lefschetz mechanism behind two geometry-to-spectrum programs: local graph–diagonal geometry generates trace coefficients rather than those coefficients being inserted to mimic an explicit formula.
limits: The flow formula requires graph–diagonal transversality and yields return-map determinants, whereas the finite-field formula uses algebraic correspondences and cohomology. Their shared kernel mechanism neither constructs a classical zeta flow nor transfers finite-field RH to number fields.
title: Graph–diagonal intersection is the common fixed-point-to-trace mechanism

claim: Passing from elliptic endomorphisms to higher-genus self-correspondences constructs an algebra on which Frobenius can act, but that carrier alone does not force its spectrum onto the required circle. The stable extra input isolated by later proof variants is a positive correspondence defect or, abstractly, a Weil form that makes adjoints positive on algebraic correspondences.
historical_or_program_relation: The historical higher-genus obstruction and the later comparison of curve-RH proofs refine the same program: generalize not the full elliptic apparatus, but the minimal positivity interface consumed by the spectral-weight argument.
limits: A correspondence ring is not itself a positive-definite norm, and a Weil form is weaker than a complete Hodge-theoretic realization. The units do not construct an analogous positive form for the classical zeta function.
title: Correspondences provide the carrier; a positive adjoint structure supplies the weight bound

claim: The curve zeta generating function compresses extension-field point counts into reciprocal Frobenius roots, and fixed-point traces identify those roots with a linear action on the Jacobian or cohomology. This spectral identification is distinct from purity: positivity supplies the one-sided magnitude control, after which reciprocal pairing from the functional equation upgrades the bound to exact modulus.
historical_or_program_relation: The function-field solution decomposes the geometry program into two independently auditable stages—construct the spectrum from counts, then provide a positive structure strong enough to locate it.
limits: The functional equation pairs reciprocal roots but does not by itself provide the initial bound. This decomposition is established for finite-field geometry and does not identify a Frobenius or positivity structure for classical L-functions.
title: Point counting identifies the Frobenius spectrum before geometry locates it

claim: The abstract two-sided architecture of an L-function separates prime-local Euler factors from global completed reflection symmetry. For modular forms, a simultaneous Hecke eigenbasis supplies multiplicative coefficients and hence Euler factors, while modular transformation followed by Mellin completion supplies the functional equation; the two analytic constraints arise from different compatible geometric symmetries.
historical_or_program_relation: This gives a concrete reason to study zeta inside broader automorphic families: geometry and commuting correspondences can explain why both halves of the L-function package coexist, rather than treating the axioms as unrelated analytic coincidences.
limits: The mechanism applies to modular or automorphic constructions already equipped with Hecke action. Establishing modularity, identifying an appropriate spectral source, and extending the explanation to arbitrary Selberg-class objects remain separate burdens.
title: Hecke diagonalization geometrically realizes the Euler-product and functional-equation package

claim: Taking logarithms of a Rankin–Selberg Euler product turns local parameter power sums into nonnegative quadratic coefficient data. That positivity blocks cancellation at the absolute-convergence boundary, allowing Landau's theorem to transfer a global analytic boundary into uniform one-sided bounds on local Euler-factor roots.
historical_or_program_relation: The two units fit as input and consumer: Rankin–Selberg structure supplies the nonnegative coefficients, and the Landau argument explains how that positivity converts global analytic information back into local spectral control.
limits: The argument depends on the relevant Rankin–Selberg continuation, coefficient positivity, and local algebraic constraints; the cited low-degree setting does not give a universal result. A one-sided local bound is not purity and does not imply RH.
title: Rankin–Selberg squaring manufactures the positivity Landau needs to bound local spectra

claim: Distributional explicit formulas turn the prime–zero identity into test-function functionals on which RH can be expressed as a uniform sign condition. In the finite-field model, an algebraic index theorem forces the corresponding negative-semidefinite sign on degree-zero divisor intersections, showing concretely how geometry can enforce a zero-location criterion globally rather than zero by zero.
historical_or_program_relation: The relation sharpens the classical geometry program from seeking a merely spectral representation to seeking an intersection or positivity structure whose sign matches the explicit-formula quadratic functional.
limits: The accepted units do not identify the classical explicit-formula functional with a divisor intersection pairing, and sign conventions and admissible test-function constraints matter. Finite-field negativity is a model of the burden, not a transfer theorem.
title: The explicit-formula sign target has a geometric model in intersection theory

claim: Zero statistics and the explicit formula support a spectral reading of L-function zeros, but they supply only an encoding target. A credible Hilbert–Pólya or geometric model must be constructed without defining its space from the zeros and must add self-adjointness, positivity, or an index-type mechanism that actually forces zero location.
historical_or_program_relation: Random-matrix evidence, noncommutative trace proposals, and the function-field analogy jointly turn the spectral program into a falsifiable dependency map: natural construction first, trace compatibility second, and a location-forcing structure last.
limits: GUE spacing, a trace-like prime–zero formula, or successful reproduction of zero counts does not establish the required operator or its self-adjointness. The units present diagnostics and research obligations, not a classical cohomology theory.
title: A spectral encoding must be independent and location-forcing, not merely statistically accurate

claim: Petersson and general automorphic trace formulas turn averages of Hecke or Satake data into a dominant diagonal or identity-orbit contribution plus controlled geometric off-diagonal terms. The same mechanism also fixes a measure on the family: harmonic weights and nonidentity orbits are not neutral bookkeeping and can alter the low-zero statistic being estimated.
historical_or_program_relation: The resonance use of Petersson orthogonality and the Plancherel-limit program are two scales of one geometry-to-statistics pipeline; the later weighting confound specifies when its output can or cannot be read as the unweighted family's symmetry type.
limits: Petersson kernels and general orbital trace formulas have different hypotheses and geometric terms. An approximate diagonal can prove averaged moment statements without locating individual zeros, and weighted density need not equal counting-family density.
title: Trace formulas diagonalize families, but their geometric side and weights define the estimand

claim: For zeta, gamma completion, pole clearing, and recentering turn reflection across the critical line into reality of zeros of an entire even function. For a nonreal Dirichlet character, multiplying the completed L-function by its conjugate partner internalizes the dual functional equation in one self-symmetric object while preserving the union of the two original zero divisors.
historical_or_program_relation: The Dirichlet construction is a structural generalization of the xi viewpoint: self-duality can be achieved at the paired-object level when it is absent from either individual L-function.
limits: Pairing enlarges the object and forgets which factor supplied a zero; it does not create positivity, prove GRH, or turn the individual character L-function into a self-dual function.
title: Conjugate pairing extends self-dual completion without changing the zero union

claim: An approximate functional equation uses reflection symmetry to compress a central value to a conductor-scale finite coefficient sum, but repeating the reflection alone yields no further saving. In a quadratic-twist family, Mellin smoothing and a large-sieve estimate control that finite representation, while the functional equation reflects the residual moment back to the original family and closes a genuinely improving exponent bootstrap.

limits: The improvement is averaged over a twist family and depends on the large sieve, smoothing, coefficient bounds, and the stated functional equation. It does not furnish comparable cancellation for a single L-function or imply a zero-location theorem.
title: Functional symmetry compresses a value once; family cancellation makes the compression improve

In level families, conditioning on the root-number sign activates a factored prime–Kloosterman off-diagonal contribution that cancels in the mixed family and produces the parity-dependent low-density kernel; ramified parity is therefore an information channel separate from leading local equidistribution or persistent central rank.

limits: The full moment recipe is conjectural, whereas the density mechanism has its own support and prime-sum hypotheses. Root-number parity controls forced central behavior and a specific off-diagonal term, not the entire low-zero distribution.
title: Root-number parity selects the off-diagonal term that distinguishes orthogonal geometries

In the corrected multiple Dirichlet series, local correction polynomials similarly place a cubic L-function sum and its reciprocal-index sum in one two-variable object, allowing two different functional equations to transport residues between polar loci.

limits: The corrected series is a two-variable meromorphic object, not merely a completed one-variable L-function. The accepted units announce rather than prove the functional equations, leave cases and local algebra omitted, and do not establish that every possible polar line actually occurs.
title: Correction polynomials extend completion from one reflection to composable two-variable symmetries

claim: Honda–Tate packages a finite-field abelian variety through its Frobenius Weil number, endomorphism algebra, isogeny class, and field of definition. The Taniyama extension raises the same reciprocity pattern to a group-level object governing CM motivic Galois actions and conjugation of Shimura data, replacing many objectwise actions by one symmetry group and cocycle.

limits: The two constructions operate in different settings, and forgetting the base field can already collapse distinct Honda–Tate situations. Identifying the common extension does not prove the conjugation conjecture, supply RH, or classify non-CM motives.
title: CM reciprocity scales from individual Frobenius classes to a common motivic symmetry extension

claim: The random-matrix contribution to a zeta-moment constant is a universal geometric factor only after matrix size is matched to local zero density; the missing source-specific information is a prime Euler factor. In the Dirichlet-series representation, this split is concrete: pairwise zeta poles carry the universal singular growth, while a regular Euler product carries the arithmetic constant.
historical_or_program_relation: The characteristic-polynomial prediction highlighted in the 2003 overview is refined by arithmetic derivations and hybrid models that identify exactly what the unitary ensemble forgets, and the 2025 survey retains density matching and restoration of prime data as separate steps.
limits: The higher zeta-moment asymptotics remain conjectural; density matching does not derive an operator or a universality theorem, and neither the matrix model nor the pole extraction alone proves the arithmetic-to-geometric factorization for zeta.
title: Moment constants split into density-calibrated geometry and prime arithmetic

claim: A Gaussian model for log absolute zeta values produces the conjectural quadratic moment exponent through its moment-generating function, but this bulk limit neither fixes the arithmetic-normalized constants nor controls the entire tail. Pole-dominated small-value behavior and the change from quadratic to V log V large-deviation decay require representations beyond the local cumulant expansion.

limits: The cited tail bounds and moment heuristics have different hypotheses and parameter ranges. Agreement on the logarithmic exponent is not agreement on constants, and no single cited unit establishes a complete zeta value distribution.
title: Gaussian bulk predicts the moment exponent but not constants or extreme regimes

Truncated exponentials or Bessel generating products then package those diagonal pairings into the same variance exponential that a Gaussian cumulant calculation produces.

title: Prime-frequency pairing is the arithmetic surrogate for Gaussian moments

Sharp use of either direction requires choosing the moment order and prime-block truncation according to variance, deviation size, and the admissible polynomial or interval length.

limits: These are inequality bridges, not an equivalence of distributions. Their conditional assumptions, smoothing, shift geometry, and interval constraints differ, and an optimizer outside the admissible length range gives only a heuristic scale.
title: Moments and tails convert in both directions only with scale-adapted budgets

title: Long polynomials reveal a length-graded filtration of off-diagonal moment terms

title: The off-diagonal pair-correlation barrier is a shifted-prime correlation problem

Widening the support asks for richer spacing information but simultaneously lengthens the arithmetic polynomial until diagonal control no longer closes.

limits: Support-restricted statistics do not determine the full zero process or unrestricted gap distribution. The cited pair- and n-level results use different hypotheses and normalizations, and the diagonalization mechanism fails rather than automatically extending when the support budget is exceeded.
title: Fourier support is an arithmetic complexity budget for zero statistics

Low-zero family statistics add separate rank and root-number channels, and changing from counting measure to a trace-formula weight can alter the observed density without changing the underlying representation type.

limits: The units concern different families and observables, and several distributional statements are predictions or GRH-compatible bounds rather than full limit theorems. A weighted density cannot be identified with the unweighted symmetry type until the weights are removed or controlled.
title: Symmetry survives in centers and moment constants, but averaging weights can mimic it

At that microscopic scale, two shifted observables retain partial correlation and coalescing shifts behave like one higher moment; when the observation is conditioned at a zero, a spherical-Bessel crossover interpolates from derivative moments at zero displacement toward ordinary field moments as the scaled displacement grows.

limits: The two crossovers have different conditioning and are not a single proved zeta theorem. The zeta transfer is conjectural, interchange of limits needs uniformity, and the recorded far-offset passage has a domain gap for scaled parameters beyond the displayed range.
title: Inverse-density shifts decide whether moments separate or coalesce

Once an analytic mean-value theorem exposes dependence on coefficient profiles, zero-density progress becomes constrained optimization: a quadratic Euler-Lagrange problem for one profile, a six-component scalar objective for multi-piece mollifiers, or a polynomial approximation to a limiting sinh profile for high derivative order.
historical_or_program_relation: Conrey's variational closure of Levinson's method becomes a reusable interface: later work enlarges the mollifier into interacting pieces and reuses the same mean-square constant to optimize derivative-zero densities.
limits: The optimization is licensed only by the stated mollifier-length and uniform-shift estimates. Continuous optimizers or displayed numerical witnesses need admissible polynomial approximation and do not certify a global optimum; the conclusions are aggregate zero proportions, not pointwise zero locations.
title: Mollified mean squares turn zero counts into constrained variational objectives

Matching the same singular parts in different coordinates yields residue identities, while for quadratic families a further averaging variable moves the mean-value problem to the residue of a corrected multiple Dirichlet series at w=1.

limits: The height and family problems are not interchangeable. Extracting the diagonal residue does not supply reflected polar terms, analytic continuation, Tauberian hypotheses, or the final moment theorem, and the central quadratic-family specialization remains an explicit proof burden.
title: Moment asymptotics are encoded by universal poles plus regular arithmetic residues

Extreme-value arguments use the same geometry operationally: prime blocks are variance-matched, a shared low-frequency trunk is removed when changing window scale, and second-moment or entropy-amplitude optimization counts paths that remain high across blocks rather than isolated terminal spikes.

limits: A finite-dimensional Gaussian limit is not a pathwise field and does not imply an extreme-value law. The tree representation proves covariance positivity, not zeta maxima; the cited maximum and free-energy results use additional mollification, comparison, moment, and scale-specific estimates.
title: Shared prime ancestry links mesoscopic covariance to multiscale extreme-value proofs

Wirtinger inequalities then consume value and derivative moments as global integral data and convert them into lower bounds for exceptional normalized gaps between critical-line zeros.

Random-matrix constants make the inequality numerically evaluable but do not prove the zeta input or RH, and moment inequalities force some large gaps without determining the full spacing law.
title: Derivative moments form an operational interface from microscopic zeros to large gaps

Structured non-Gaussian deviations and slow convergence of low-zero or local-maximum data are therefore compatible with asymptotic unitary universality rather than immediate counterexamples to it.

limits: Finite-N agreement is supportive modeling evidence, not a proof of zeta universality. Random matrices omit prime arithmetic, the cited numerical observables are not identical, and slow convergence cannot be invoked to explain away arbitrary discrepancies.
title: Finite matrix size is a density calibration, not disposable error

claim: The Selberg calculation and the coordinate-free flow calculation expose the same concrete source of periodic-orbit weights: restricting a propagator kernel from a flow graph to the diagonal produces a Jacobian, expressed for a closed orbit through the inverse determinant of one minus its Poincare return map. In the hyperbolic quotient this becomes the primitive-length, repetition, and stability weight in the smoothed Selberg trace formula; a resulting wave-trace singularity can then force a lower bound on averaged spectral-counting fluctuation.

None supplies a zeta Hamiltonian or identifies Riemann zeros as a self-adjoint spectrum.
title: Trace-formula orbit weights arise from graph-diagonal geometry

Passing the alpha=1 boundary exposes the off-diagonal sums of shifted von Mangoldt values; an independent near-diagonal phase analysis reaches the same shifted mean after prime powers are compressed into Lambda(n). title: Extending zero-correlation bandwidth forces shifted-prime input

claim: Cutoff kernel summation can reduce an S-local or one-place scaling trace to explicit principal-value terms, with logarithmic differentiation turning multiplicative scaling into additive local contributions. The remaining Weil-positivity program is nevertheless globally coupled: principal-value constants at different places must be coordinated, and the proposed coordinator is the global Poisson formula rather than an arbitrary collection of locally valid normalizations.
